glossary_intro: The terms, symbols, and printing details on Riftbound cards and across OpenRift. Entries link to the comprehensive rules.
glossary_domains_intro: Riftbound has six domains, each with its own colour and symbol: Fury, Calm, Mind, Body, Chaos, and Order. A card's domain is shown by glyphs in the lower-right corner of the card, and runes of that domain produce the Power needed to pay its costs. Your Champion Legend's domains determine your deck's Domain Identity, which limits which other cards you can include.
glossary_card_types_intro: A card's type tells you how and where it interacts with the game. Units fight on battlefields, Gear attaches to a Unit you control, Spells resolve their effects and leave play, Runes sit in your Rune Pool to produce Energy and Power, Battlefields are the locations Units fight over, and Legends sit beside your deck and represent your Champion.
glossary_supertypes_intro: Supertypes apply on top of a card's type and are listed before it on the card face. They mostly affect deckbuilding.
glossary_supertype_champion_description: Applies exclusively to Units. Determines who can be your Chosen Champion.
glossary_supertype_signature_description: Can apply to any card type. Limited to 3 per deck, tied to your Champion's tag.
glossary_supertype_token_description: Temporary game objects created by effects, not part of a deck.
glossary_keywords_intro: Keywords are short words or phrases that stand in for a longer rule. They appear in card text in square brackets, like [Equip] or [Deathknell]. Tap a rule reference to jump to the full definition.
glossary_symbols_intro: Riftbound uses a small set of inline symbols on cards to express costs and core game concepts compactly.
glossary_symbol_might_summary: A unit's combat power. Higher Might deals more damage and is harder to remove.
glossary_symbol_might_bonus_summary: A boxed Might value on Gear, indicating how much Might the gear adds to its equipped unit.
glossary_symbol_exhaust_summary: Turning a card, rune, or legend sideways to use it. Once exhausted, it can't be exhausted again until something readies it.
glossary_symbol_recycle_summary: Place a card or rune from the board onto the bottom of its deck. Often used to pay Power costs.
glossary_symbol_power_activation_summary: Exhaust a rune of a specific domain to add its Power to your Rune Pool, then spend it to pay costs.
glossary_symbol_energy_summary: Pay Energy by exhausting any rune, regardless of domain. Shown as a numeric cost on the card.
glossary_symbol_rune_rainbow_summary: Marked [A]. A Power cost that can be paid with a rune of any domain. This is the wild Power symbol.
glossary_rarities_intro: Every printing has a rarity, shown by the coloured glyph in the middle of the card face. Rarity reflects how often a card appears in booster packs and the visual treatment of its frame, not its strength in play. The Showcase tier is reserved for premium full-art and alternative-art printings.
glossary_booster_intro_before: A standard Riftbound booster contains 14 cards across five slot types. The
glossary_booster_rates_note: Headline rates come from Riot's Origins announcement. Foil-slot and cascade rates are community estimates.
glossary_pack_slot_rare_description: Each flex slot rolls Epic about 13.4% of the time and Rare otherwise, which works out to roughly 1 in 4 packs containing at least one Epic.
glossary_pack_slot_foil_description: Usually a Common (~70%) or Uncommon (~25%) foil, occasionally upgrading to a Rare (~4%) or Epic (~1%) foil. The whole slot can be replaced by a Showcase alt-art (~1 per 12 packs), an overnumbered Showcase (1 per 72 packs), a signed Showcase (1 per 720 packs), or an Ultimate (~0.1% of packs, where the pool has one).
glossary_pack_slot_rune_description: Usually a basic Rune. Occasionally a foil Rune, sometimes a Token-supertype card (e.g. Sprite, Recruit), and very rarely an alt-art Rune.
glossary_art_variants_intro: An art variant describes which illustration appears on a printing. Alt-art printings are usually marked by a lowercase letter suffix on the card number, like OGN-120a.
glossary_art_variant_altart: An additional artwork using the same card name and rarity. Distinguished by a lowercase letter suffix on the card number (e.g. 120a).
glossary_art_variant_overnumbered: Reprinted art with a card number that exceeds the printed set total, typically a special variant slotted into a later set.
glossary_art_variant_ultimate: A premium full-art treatment. The card itself usually keeps its original rarity (e.g. Showcase), since Ultimate describes the artwork, not the rarity.
glossary_finishes_intro: Finish describes the physical production treatment of a printing. Most cards use a normal cardstock finish, foil printings add a glossy reflective coating across the card face, and a small number have been released as premium metal collectibles. Finish is independent of rarity and art variant, so the same artwork can exist as both a normal and a foil printing.
glossary_finish_normal: Standard cardstock with no special treatment.
glossary_finish_foil: Glossy foil finish across the card face.
glossary_finish_metal_deluxe: Higher-tier metal printing with extra finishing.
glossary_markers_intro: Markers describe how a printing was distributed rather than what's on the card. They cover promotional channels like prereleases, tournaments, judge programs, and store-level events, and a single printing can carry more than one.
glossary_printing_details_intro: Artist credit is tracked per printing so reprints can preserve the original illustrator, and the signature flag marks printings where the artist's signature is overlaid on the artwork (usually on a foil alt-art or Ultimate variant).
glossary_printing_detail_artist_descript: Illustrator credit printed on the card. Tracked per printing so reprints can credit the original artist.
glossary_printing_detail_signature_descr: A printing flag indicating the card carries the artist's signature, usually overlaid on a foil alt-art or Ultimate variant.
glossary_sets_intro_before: Sets are how Riftbound releases new cards. Each set has a three-letter code that prefixes every card number in it, and is classified as either a main set (the regular release cadence) or a supplemental set (smaller drops outside the main schedule). Browse the full catalogue of any set on the
glossary_numbering_intro: Every printing has a short code combining the three-letter set code with a card number, like OGN-007.
glossary_numbering_base: Set code followed by the printed card number.
glossary_numbering_altart: A lowercase letter suffix marks an alt-art variant of the same base card. Distinct from the Showcase rarity, which is shown by the rarity glyph in the middle of the card.
glossary_numbering_overnumbered: A number above the set's printed total is an Overnumbered variant, usually a special reprint slotted into a later set.
glossary_numbering_token: T prefix indicates a token printed for the set. T and R prefixes were introduced with Spiritforged. Origins used standard numbering for tokens and runes.
glossary_numbering_rune: R prefix indicates a rune printed for the set (introduced in Spiritforged).

help_collections_intro: A collection is where your cards physically live. Think of it as a real-world location: "Red Deck Box", "Binder 1", "Main Storage Box", or even "Lent to Sebastian". Every copy in your collection lives in exactly one place.
help_collections_physical_p1: Collections mirror where your cards actually are in the real world. Moving a copy from "Inbox" to "Red Deck Box" records that you physically put that card in that box.
help_collections_physical_p2_mid: (specific physical cards), not the cards as game concepts. If you own three copies of the same card, each one lives in a collection, whether that's the same collection or different ones. See
help_collections_physical_p2_after: for more on how these relate.
help_collections_availability_p1_before: Each collection has an "available for deck building" toggle. Open a collection, hit the three-dot menu, and pick
help_collections_availability_p1_after: to change it. When turned off, copies in that collection don't count toward owned cards in the deck builder or the shopping list.
help_collections_availability_p2: This is useful for cards you don't want to cannibalise: a high-value card you keep in a display case, cards lent to a friend, or copies already committed to a specific deck. Locked-away copies still show up in the deck builder's ownership panel as "locked", so you can see what you'd have available if you turned the collection back on.
help_collections_start_p1_mid: from the top navigation. Your first collection is the
help_collections_start_p1_after: , which is always present. It's where quick-added cards land unless you choose a different target.
help_collections_start_p2_before: To create a new collection, click
help_collections_start_p2_after: in the sidebar, type a name, and press Enter. Name it after the real-world location where you keep those cards.
help_collections_adding_lead: There are a few ways to add cards to a collection:
help_collections_adding_quick_desc: A fast search palette. Type a card name, use arrow keys to navigate, and press Enter to add. Shift+Enter to undo.
help_collections_adding_browse_desc: Browse the full catalog with all filters available. Click the plus button on any card to add it. A pulsing red dot shows you're in add mode.
help_collections_adding_several_desc: Click a card in the grid to select it, then press a number key to add that many copies in one press. Plus and minus add or remove one.
help_collections_adding_done_before: Both modes track what you've added during the session. Click
help_collections_organizing_drag_desc: Drag cards from the grid onto a collection or a list in the sidebar. A blue ring highlights the target. One copy comes along by default: hold a number key while dragging to bring that many, or Shift for the whole stack.
help_collections_organizing_bulk_desc: Click the checkbox icon in the toolbar, or Ctrl-click any card to start selecting. A floating action bar appears at the bottom.
help_collections_organizing_move_desc: Select cards, then click Move. Pick the target collection from the dialog and confirm. Each copy belongs to exactly one collection, so moving it removes it from the source.
help_collections_organizing_dispose_desc: Select cards, then click Dispose to permanently remove them. The removal is recorded in your activity history.
help_collections_views_p: Collections support the same three view modes as the card browser. You can also filter, sort, and group cards inside any collection just like in the catalog.
help_collections_views_cards_detail: One entry per unique card. Owned count sums across all printings of that card.
help_collections_views_printings_detail: One entry per printing. See exactly which versions you own.
help_collections_views_copies_detail: Every individual copy on the grid, no stacking. Useful for managing specific copies.

help_collections_sidebar_p1_mid1: shows everything you own across all collections in one view, including your total collection value from your preferred marketplace. Below your collections are links to
help_collections_sidebar_p1_mid2: (bring cards in from a CSV or plain list) and
help_collections_sidebar_p1_after: (a log of all additions, moves, and removals). Export sits in each collection's three-dot menu.

help_collections_sidebar_p2_after: toggle at the foot of their section, which keeps a long sidebar down to what you actually use. On a phone, press and hold instead of right-clicking.

help_proxy_printing_intro: Proxy printing lets you generate a printable PDF of cards from any deck, perfect for playtesting before you buy. Cards are laid out at standard size (63×88 mm), nine per page, ready to cut and sleeve.
help_proxy_printing_layout_caption: 3×3 grid, 9 cards per page, centered on A4 or US Letter
help_proxy_printing_start_intro: There are two ways to open the proxy printing:
help_proxy_printing_step_editor_descript: Open a deck in the editor, open the three-dot menu in the top bar, and choose Print. Proxies are the first tab of the print dialog.
help_proxy_printing_step_list_descriptio: On the Decks page, open the three-dot menu on any deck tile and choose Print.
help_proxy_printing_option_render_descri: Card images shows the actual card art. Text placeholders shows a simplified card with name, stats, and rules text, which can be easier to read during playtesting.
help_proxy_printing_option_page_descript: Choose A4 (210 × 297 mm) or US Letter (8.5 × 11 in). Cards are centered on the page regardless of size.
help_proxy_printing_option_cut_descripti: Adds light gray lines along the edges of each card to guide you when cutting. Helpful if you're not using a paper cutter.
help_proxy_printing_option_watermark_des: Stamps each card with a small 'PROXY' badge so they can't be mistaken for real cards. Enabled by default.
help_proxy_printing_generate_after: to start. The dialog shows a progress indicator as each unique card is rendered. Once all cards are ready, they're assembled into a multi-page PDF and downloaded automatically.
help_proxy_printing_generate_copies: Cards with multiple copies in your deck appear the correct number of times in the PDF (a 3× card takes up three slots). Each unique card is only rendered once and then reused, so even large decks generate quickly.
help_proxy_printing_limits_body: Right now, proxy printing requires a deck. You can't yet print arbitrary cards from your collection or a custom selection. The deck editor also picks a default printing for each card, so you can't choose which specific art or edition appears on the proxy. I'm working on improving this so you can select concrete printings and print proxies without needing a deck.
help_proxy_printing_printing_body: Make sure scaling is set to 100% or "Actual size" in your print dialog, otherwise the cards won't be standard size. After cutting, slip each proxy in front of a basic card inside an opaque sleeve for the right weight and feel.

help_browser_extension_intro: OpenRift Companion is a small Firefox extension that does two things. It sends the decklist you're looking at on another site to OpenRift's import page, and it marks a Cardmarket seller's offers with how many copies you own and how many you still want. Clicking the icon in the toolbar opens a popup with the one action that fits the page you're on.
help_browser_extension_install_intro: Mozilla signs the add-on, but I host it myself instead of listing it on addons.mozilla.org, so installing takes one extra confirmation.
help_browser_extension_install_step_1_de: Open the link below in Firefox. It hands you the add-on file directly.
help_browser_extension_install_step_2_de: Firefox asks whether to add it and lists what it may access. Adding it puts an OpenRift icon in the toolbar.
help_browser_extension_install_step_3_de: Optional, but worth it: open the puzzle-piece menu and pin OpenRift so the popup is one click away.
help_browser_extension_install_updates: Updates take care of themselves. Firefox checks for a newer signed build roughly once a day, so you only ever do this once.
help_browser_extension_import_step_1_des: Any page on another site showing the deck you want, on the tab you're reading.
help_browser_extension_import_step_2_tit: Click the icon, then Import deck
help_browser_extension_import_step_2_des: It reads the deck from that page, once, and opens OpenRift's import page in a new tab.
help_browser_extension_import_step_3_des: The deck name comes from the page heading, and the page's own address is offered as a deck link you can keep or drop. Check the cards it matched, then save.
help_browser_extension_import_signed_out: Signed out, the deck is saved in your browser and moves to your account the next time you sign in.
help_browser_extension_read_tables_desc: A table of card names and quantities, with zones kept apart. The common shape on deck sites.
help_browser_extension_read_lists_desc: A plain list of names under section headings. Sideboards stay separate; card-type groupings fold into the main deck.
help_browser_extension_read_codes_desc: A deck code in the address, in the text, or behind a link. It's decoded to check it really is one before anything happens.
help_browser_extension_read_none_desc: The popup says so and stops there. Copy the list by hand into the import page instead.
help_browser_extension_counts_intro: Nothing about the seller, the page, or what you look at goes back to OpenRift. Your counts travel the other way, and the matching happens inside the Cardmarket page.
help_browser_extension_counts_step_1_aft: , every wishlist starts ticked. Untick the ones you don't want counted.
help_browser_extension_counts_step_2_des: Once you've allowed it access, it takes them as the page opens. Otherwise click the OpenRift icon while that page is open.
help_browser_extension_counts_step_3_bef: Every card you own or want is marked
help_browser_extension_counts_step_3_aft: , with your own price beside the seller's asking price. Cards you neither own nor want are left alone.
help_browser_extension_counts_price: The price shown is whichever marketplace sits first in your marketplace order, the same one OpenRift prices your cards with everywhere else. The seller's asking price is tinted against it: green at or under, amber up to a fifth over, red beyond that. Cardmarket sells in euro, so a TCGplayer price is shown but never compared.
help_browser_extension_counts_stale: Counts go stale as you buy and sell. The popup says how old they are and which wishlists they came from, and refreshes them in one click.
help_browser_extension_picks_intro: Buying from someone you know, outside Cardmarket? Pick the cards on their offers and turn them into a list you can send them.
help_browser_extension_picks_step_1_titl: Press + on the cards you want
help_browser_extension_picks_step_1_desc: Every card on a seller's offers gets a small + and − next to it. Press + once per copy. The count on the OpenRift icon keeps the total across pages.
help_browser_extension_picks_step_2_desc: Open the popup and choose Send to OpenRift next to the seller's name. A review page opens with your picks matched to cards, and the picks leave the extension.
help_browser_extension_picks_step_3_titl: Save the list and share it
help_browser_extension_picks_step_3_desc: Fix anything that did not match, then save. Picks go to an organize list, so your wishlists stay untouched, and the list's share link is what you send the seller.
help_browser_extension_access_p1: Installing it asks for nothing but the tab you're on, in the moment you act. It has no list of sites, so it can't run in the background and never sees your browsing history.
help_browser_extension_access_p2: For the Cardmarket counts you can grant it two sites, www.cardmarket.com and this one, from the popup or its options page. A fresh install opens that page so the choice isn't buried. Granting them buys one thing: it stops needing the click. Offers pages get marked as they load, and your counts are picked up whenever the counts page opens. Decline and everything still works, one page at a time, from the popup.
help_browser_extension_firefox_only: Firefox only for now. A Chrome version is built and works, but Chrome allows no way to install one outside its Web Store, and I haven't taken it through that yet.

help_why_openrift_exists_p1: Honestly? I just wanted to track my collection.
help_why_openrift_exists_p2: I used the existing Riftbound trackers for months, and each one was missing something I needed. Eventually I stopped waiting for someone else to build it and built the tool I wanted. It has become the app I use every day for my own cards.
help_why_openrift_exists_p3: I know how that sounds: the world didn't ask for yet another collection tracker. The honest answer to "why not improve an existing one instead?" is that none of them are open source, so there was nothing to contribute to. OpenRift is, and it imports from and exports to the formats the other tools use, so you can bring your collection over in minutes, and take it back out just as easily.
help_why_openrift_exists_p4_before: It's not just me, either. My local game store group uses it every day, for example to run our shared "bulk box": a group collection of spare cards where taking a card out moves it straight into your own collection. A good part of the
help_why_openrift_exists_p5_before: The fair question to ask any new fan project is whether it will still be around next year. I can't promise the future, but I can point at a track record: the
help_why_openrift_exists_p5_after: shows what has shipped week by week since launch, my play group depends on the app daily, and my own collection lives here too. As long as I play Riftbound, OpenRift gets maintained.
help_why_openrift_open_source_after: under AGPL-3.0. Inspect, fork, self-host, or open an issue. I read every single one.
help_why_openrift_no_lock_in_description: Import and export collections and decks in formats any other tool can read. If OpenRift ever stops working for you, taking your data elsewhere is easy.
help_why_openrift_private_groups_descrip: Form a private group with friends or your local store crew: shared collections (my play group runs its bulk box of spares this way) and trade matching that shows who has cards from your wishlists. The trade itself happens in person.
help_why_openrift_speed_description: Speed is the main design goal: browsing the catalog and editing decks should feel instant, on desktop and on your phone. If you catch a slow screen anywhere, that's a bug I want to hear about.
help_why_openrift_gaps_intro: An honest pitch names the gaps too. Two things first, because no feature list captures them:
help_why_openrift_new_kid_description: OpenRift is new and small. Most Riftbound players are on Piltover Archive today, and that's earned. The upside of being early here: your feature request isn't one voice among thousands. It gets read, and if it fits, it shapes the roadmap.
help_why_openrift_less_time_description: More than 12,000 automated tests and daily use keep the quality up, but years of real users find edge cases no test suite does. If you hit one, tell me: fixes ship fast.
help_why_openrift_credit_intro: And credit where it's due: the other tools genuinely do some things better.
help_why_openrift_gap_piltover_text: has bulk adding of cards, a massive library of user and tournament decklists, and by far the biggest community.
help_why_openrift_gap_riftbound_gg_text: has aggregate tournament statistics plus a steady stream of articles and guides, which OpenRift doesn't have.
help_why_openrift_gap_riftcore_text: has AI-powered tools and an Android app in the Play Store.
help_why_openrift_gaps_outro: If one of those is the feature you need today, use that tool. OpenRift imports and exports in compatible formats, so you can run it alongside another tracker, or switch back and forth, whenever you like.
help_why_openrift_unique_intro_before: These are OpenRift features with no counterpart on the other sites, as far as I know. For the full tour of everything the app does, unique or not, see the
help_why_openrift_unique_trade_text: inside a private group, see who has cards from your wishlists (and who wants your spares), with one-tap requests and email alerts. The trade itself happens in person.
help_why_openrift_unique_group_collectio: pool spare cards into a collection the whole group can see and take from.
help_why_openrift_unique_lending_text: lend a card to a friend and it stays in your collection, but stops counting for decks and trades until it comes back. A lending page tracks who has what, including cards you're borrowing.
help_why_openrift_unique_deck_boxes_text: point a deck at the collection its cards physically live in. The deck page then fills the box from your copies, and flags what the box still holds that the deck no longer needs.
help_why_openrift_unique_companion_text: a Firefox add-on that reads the decklist on whatever site you are looking at and hands it to the import page, name and source link included. No copying, no export step, and it works while you are logged out.
help_why_openrift_unique_tournament_text: run a casual event yourself, with pod scoring and standings, deck submission via a per-event link, and judge deck-check tools.
help_why_openrift_unique_match_tracker_t: keep score for two to four players during a game on your phone, with points, XP, and an undo for the mis-tapped ones. It works offline and saves nothing to your account.
help_why_openrift_unique_discord_before: look up a card, a deck, or a rule in your own server with a slash command or by writing
help_why_openrift_unique_discord_after: , and post a group's tradelists into a channel.
help_why_openrift_unique_quick_entry_tex: add cards by name from a fast keyboard palette, without browsing: type, press Enter to add, Shift+Enter to undo.
help_why_openrift_unique_completion_text: a chart showing which missing cards give you the most completion progress if added next.
help_why_openrift_unique_pack_opener_tex: open virtual boosters at the real published pull rates, one card at a time or a whole display.

help_how_to_play_intro: Riftbound is a two-player trading card game from Riot Games. Two champions clash across a row of battlefields, and the first to score enough points wins. This is a quick primer, not the full rulebook. For the official rules, see the links at the bottom.
help_how_to_play_goal_after: (11 in team play) to win. You score by controlling battlefields. Take a battlefield to bank a point, then earn one more point each turn you keep it.
help_how_to_play_bring_heading: What you bring to the table
help_how_to_play_bring_intro: Each player builds a kit around a single legend. The legend sets your two domains (colors), and every other card has to fit those domains.
help_how_to_play_zone_legend_description: Your champion legend. Defines the deck's two domains.
help_how_to_play_zone_champion_descripti: A champion unit that shares a tag with your legend.
help_how_to_play_zone_battlefields_descr: Three unique battlefields. Brought to the table by both players.
help_how_to_play_zone_runes_description: A separate side deck of resources, not your main draw pile.
help_how_to_play_zone_main_deck_descript: Units, spells, and gear. Your champion counts toward the 40.
help_how_to_play_deck_builder_after: enforces all of this for you in Constructed format.
help_how_to_play_board_after: where their units deploy. Between the players sits a row of battlefields, contributed from both kits but up for grabs by either player once the game starts.
help_how_to_play_board_diagram: [Diagram: opponent base on top, three battlefields in the middle, your base on the bottom, runes and decks to the side]
help_how_to_play_turn_intro: Players alternate turns. Each turn moves through three phases.
help_how_to_play_step_start_description: Draw a card. Gain two new runes from your rune deck. Ready any cards that were exhausted last turn.
help_how_to_play_step_action_description: Spend power to play units, gear, and spells. Move units to battlefields. Most of the game happens here, with both players passing actions back and forth.
help_how_to_play_step_end_description: Cleanup. Damage on units resets, and play passes to your opponent.
help_how_to_play_runes_intro: Runes are your resource. They live in a separate 12-card deck and you gain two new ones every turn. There are two ways to spend a rune.
help_how_to_play_rune_exhaust_descriptio: Exhaust a rune to pay for a normal card cost. It readies again at the start of your next turn.
help_how_to_play_rune_return_description: Return a rune to your rune deck to pay for stronger effects. It is gone for the rest of the turn.
help_how_to_play_battlefields_intro: Battlefields are how you score, so they are where the fights happen.
help_how_to_play_term_move_in_detail: Units deploy to your base, then move to a battlefield. Some units have Ganking, which lets them hop between battlefields without going home first.
help_how_to_play_term_showdown_detail: When both players have units at the same battlefield, every unit there deals damage equal to its Might at the same time. A unit dies if damage meets or exceeds its Might.
help_how_to_play_term_conquer_detail: Hold a battlefield with no opposing units present and you score a point. You score one more for every turn you keep it.
help_how_to_play_domains_intro: Domains are Riftbound's colors. Every legend has two, and your deck can only use cards from those two domains plus colorless. Each domain has a flavor.
help_how_to_play_keywords_text: Cards use short keywords (Shield, Deflect, Ganking, Accelerate, and more) as shorthand for rules text. You don't need to memorize them upfront. The starter decks introduce a handful at a time, and the rest you pick up by reading cards as they show up.
help_how_to_play_reading_text: Most cards show an energy cost in the top corner, a name and type, an effect, and (for units) a Might value used in Showdowns. Costs include both colored pips, which require runes of that domain, and generic pips, which any rune can pay for.

help_tournament_api_field_external_id_af: are reserved for decks players submit themselves and are rejected.
help_tournament_api_field_player_name_be: : shown to judges next to the entry.
help_tournament_api_field_player_name_af: are optional and also shown to judges.
help_tournament_api_field_consent_before: : the player's consent to publish their deck, name, and Riot ID after the event. Send
help_tournament_api_field_consent_after: when a player declined; omit a flag to keep what is already stored (new entries default to allowed).
help_tournament_api_field_withdrawn_afte: to withdraw a player. Pushing the entry again without the flag restores them.
help_tournament_api_field_cards: : one line per card with its English name as printed, the quantity, and the deck section.
help_tournament_api_sections_before: Sections map onto OpenRift's deck zones:
help_tournament_api_sections_after: and plurals work too; any other section rejects the whole push, so nothing is half-imported. Card names don't have to resolve, though: a misspelled or unknown name never blocks a push, the line is flagged and judges see the raw name exactly as you sent it.
help_tournament_api_changes_before: Pushes are partial: only the entries you send are touched, and leaving a player out of a push never withdraws them. Withdrawing is always the explicit
help_tournament_api_changes_after: flag. That makes pushes safe to repeat: re-sending an unchanged entry does nothing, so you can push on every registration event without bookkeeping.
help_tournament_api_changes_replace: When a re-pushed entry's card list actually changed, the stored deck is replaced. If a judge had already checked that deck, the check is reset and the judge sees exactly which cards were added, removed, or changed, so a stale check can never pass a changed deck. Your system stays the source of truth for the list: a push also replaces any edits the player made in OpenRift in the meantime.
help_tournament_api_response_before: A successful push returns counts of what happened plus one result per entry, keyed by your own
help_tournament_api_response_entry_befor: is the stable OpenRift id for the entry.
help_tournament_api_response_entry_after: is a personal link for that player: put it in your confirmation email. A player who opens it signs in (or creates an account), confirms, and from then on sees their own submitted deck in OpenRift, and only their own. Nothing about the deck or the player is visible before the claim is confirmed, and OpenRift never needs the player's email address for this.
help_tournament_api_response_stable_link: The link is stable: re-pushing the same entry returns the same URL, so it is safe to re-send in a follow-up email. If a link ever reaches the wrong person, a judge can unlink the entry, which also blocks it from being claimed again.
help_tournament_api_limits_before: A push carries at most 500 entries with up to 200 card lines each, the body is capped at 1 MB, and each key may push 60 times per minute (responses include standard
help_tournament_api_limits_after: headers). Larger fields simply split across several pushes.
help_tournament_api_error_400: The body is not valid JSON or doesn't match the payload shape.
help_tournament_api_error_401: The API key is missing, unknown, or revoked.
help_tournament_api_error_404: No tournament with that id belongs to the key's host, or the tournament has deck submission turned off.
help_tournament_api_error_409: The tournament is archived. Un-archive it before pushing.
help_tournament_api_error_413: The body is larger than 1 MB.
help_tournament_api_error_422: A card uses an unknown section, or an external id starts with the reserved “openrift:” prefix. Nothing from the push is imported.
help_tournament_api_error_429: More than 60 pushes in a minute with this key. Wait and retry.
help_tournament_api_failed_note: Failed pushes import nothing, so it is always safe to fix the problem and send the same push again.

help_import_export_status_exact_detail: Perfect match: code, finish, and art variant all resolved. Ready to import.
help_import_export_status_review_detail: OpenRift found a likely match but isn't sure (e.g. multiple printings fit, or only a similar name was found). Use the dropdown to confirm or pick the right one.
help_import_export_status_unresolved_det: No match found. This row won't be imported.

For entries that need review, use the dropdown to pick the correct printing, or click the search icon to look up any printing in the catalog. You can also
help_import_export_review_p2_before: Finally, pick a target collection (or create a new one), and click
help_import_export_review_p2_after: . A summary at the bottom shows how many copies are ready and how many need attention. Don't import the same file twice: OpenRift tracks individual copies, so a second import adds duplicates rather than updating totals.

help_cards_printings_copies_cards_p1_aft: is the game concept itself: the name, rules text, type, domains, stats, and keywords. It's the same card regardless of which set or art it appears in. "Fury Rune" is a card no matter how many times it has been printed.
help_cards_printings_copies_cards_p2_aft: view shows one entry per unique card. Use it to answer "do I have this card at all?" The detail panel lists every available printing under
help_cards_printings_copies_printings_p1: is a specific physical version of a card. It belongs to a set (like Origins or Spiritforged) and has its own short code, rarity, finish, art variant, artist, language, and printed text. Each printing has its own image and market price.
help_cards_printings_copies_printings_p2: The short code is visible at the bottom left of the physical card, like
. Two printings can share the same short code and still be different, for example a normal finish and a foil finish, or a special promo edition.
help_cards_printings_copies_printings_p3: Printed text can vary too: some alt art cards omit reminder text, newer printings may carry updated wording after an errata, and flavor text often differs.
help_cards_printings_copies_printings_p4: view shows every version separately, each with its own image, rarity, and price. Use this when you care about specific editions.
help_cards_printings_copies_copies_p1_be: Every time you add a card to your collection, you're recording a
help_cards_printings_copies_copies_p1_af: of a specific printing. Three of the same foil printing means three copies. In the real world, each copy could have its own condition details (like a PSA grading or a coffee stain), but those aren't tracked yet.

help_groups_intro: A group is a small, closed circle of OpenRift users, like a regular playgroup, your locals, or a Discord trade channel. Inside a group, members share wishlists and tradelists with each other, pool cards into group collections, share their personal binders for others to peek at, and see matches when one member's wants overlap with another's haves.
help_groups_glance_eyebrow: A group page at a glance
help_groups_alert_p1: Joining a group always requires an admin to approve. Nobody can see your lists by joining anonymously.
help_groups_alert_p2: Sharing a list with a group is per-list and per-group. Sharing your wishlist with "Tuesday Crew" doesn't share it with "Cube Night", and unsharing later only affects that one group. The list itself never leaves your account, only the contents become visible to the members of that one group.
help_groups_roles_intro: Every member has one of three roles. Each group has exactly one owner.
help_groups_roles_owner_detail: Everything an admin can do, plus delete the group and transfer ownership. The role stays with the person who created the group until they hand it off.
help_groups_roles_admin_detail: Approve or deny join requests, turn the invite link on or off, edit the group's name and description, promote members, and remove members.
help_groups_roles_member_detail: Share their own lists, create shared collections, choose which contact methods to share, and leave the group at any time.
help_groups_start_p1_s3: from the top navigation and click
help_groups_start_step_1_title: Name it after the playgroup, not the cards
help_groups_start_step_1_desc: The name shows up to every member. Pick something they'll recognize like 'Tuesday Night Crew' or 'Hamburg locals'.
help_groups_start_step_2_desc: Used in the URL: /groups/<slug>. Lowercase letters, digits, and dashes. You can rename it later, but old bookmarks will break.
help_groups_start_step_3_desc: Leave invites on to get a link and QR code you can hand out. Turn them off to close the group to newcomers. You can turn the link off later, and turning invites back on hands out a different link.
help_groups_join_intro: You join someone else's group through their invite link, and an admin has to let you in.
help_groups_join_link_desc: Open the link an admin sent you, or scan their QR code. The page previews the group before you commit, and sends a join request to its admins.
help_groups_join_approval_desc: Your request waits under 'Awaiting approval' on the Groups page. You're a member once an admin approves it, and you can cancel it before then.
help_groups_share_intro_after: , and tick the lists you want to share. Untick to stop sharing. Wishlists and tradelists feed the matches section. Organize lists are visible to members but don't generate matches.
help_groups_share_wishlist_desc: What you're looking for. Shows up under 'Members have what you want' when a tradelist matches.
help_groups_share_tradelist_desc: What you're offering. Shows up under 'Members want what you have' when a wishlist matches.
help_groups_share_organize_desc: Reference lists you want members to see. Informational only, doesn't generate matches.
help_groups_matches_intro: The Matches section at the top of the group page shows two views:
help_groups_matches_have_text: : a member is offering a card on a tradelist they've shared with the group, and the card is on a wishlist you've shared with the group.
help_groups_matches_p2_before: Click a member name on any match row to jump to their profile inside the group, which shows every match you have with that specific person. If a section is empty, it's either because nobody's shared the relevant kind of list yet, or because nothing actually overlaps right now. See
help_groups_matches_p2_after: for how matches handle different printings of the same card.
help_groups_matches_p3_after: under More → Organize lists everyone you're trading with across all your groups, with the people waiting on you first. Its badge in the menu counts people, not cards.
help_groups_group_collections_p1: A group collection is a pooled inventory that any member of the group can add to or remove from. It's useful for a club cube, a draft pool, or a binder you run together with friends.
help_groups_group_collections_p2_before: Group collections appear in your own collection sidebar alongside your private collections, with a group badge so you can tell them apart. They behave the same way as any other collection: cards can be moved in and out, filtered, searched, and printed as proxies. See
help_groups_personal_p1_before: You can also let group members peek at one of your own personal binders without giving up control. Open a collection's share dialog and tick the groups you want to share it with under
help_groups_personal_p1_after: . Members see a read-only view of the cards, just like an anonymous share link, but only while they're signed in and a member of the group.
help_groups_personal_p2_before: On the group page, every shared personal binder is listed under
help_groups_personal_p2_after: , subgrouped by owner. Click one to open its read-only browser. Leaving the group, or unticking the group in the share dialog, immediately revokes access.
help_groups_members_p1: The Members section lists everyone in the group with their role. Click a member to open their profile inside this group, which shows their shared lists and your matches with them specifically.
help_groups_members_p2_after: once in your profile (Discord, Signal, phone, email, or wherever people reach you), then open a group's settings to choose which of them to share with that group. Shared contacts appear next to your name on the Members and Trades pages, visible only to that group's members, so the people you're trading with know how to reach you.
help_groups_leaving_leave_text: members and admins can leave at any time from the group's Settings panel. Your shared lists detach automatically. The lists themselves stay on your account.
help_groups_leaving_transfer_text: owners can hand the role to any other member from the member action menu. Once transferred, you become a regular admin and can then leave like anyone else.
help_groups_leaving_delete_text: only the owner can delete a group. Members, invites, list-shares, and the shared-collection metadata are all removed. Members' private lists and their copies inside shared collections are unaffected.

marketing_features_catalog_title: All the cards, easy to browse
marketing_features_catalog_description: OpenRift aims to have all cards and promos catalogued in all available languages. Currently that means English, Chinese, French, and Korean printings and around 800 promos. We have exhaustive filtering and sorting options, so you can easily find the cards you're looking for.
marketing_features_import_description: Moving in from another tool, or just want to try things out? You can start your OpenRift collection by pasting a plain text list or uploading a CSV from Piltover Archive, RiftCore, or RiftMana. Nothing to convert, nothing to retype. If you ever want to leave, you can export your collection back to those formats (and more).
marketing_features_scan_description: Point your camera at a card and it appears in a list on your device, with its price and whether you own it already. One button adds the whole list to a collection when you are done. The scanner works offline, is not fooled easily by bad lighting, and takes less than a second to recognize cards on modern phones. Works with desktop webcams as well. No usage limits and completely free.
marketing_features_collections_descripti: Create as many as you like: binders, storage drawers, shoe boxes, deck boxes. View them separately, or all together. Never lose track of where you put that card again.
marketing_features_lists_description: Fill a list by hand, by rule, or both. A rule is the card browser's entire filter language pointed at a list, and every dimension can exclude as well as include. A rule could be "A playset of every Origins printing I'm still missing, in English, no metal printings". Lists can combine multiple rules as well. Tradelists run the same machinery in reverse, e.g. "Keep three of each card and offer the surplus."
marketing_features_prices_description: Daily prices from TCGplayer, Cardmarket, and CardTrader on every printing, with history charts showing where a card has been heading. Your collection's total value is tracked over time too, for any marketplace and any set of your collections.
marketing_features_promos_description: Stamps like Promo, Judge and Prerelease are tracked per printing. Where the card was handed out is a separate axis, a channel tree four levels deep. You can group the page by either.
marketing_features_decks_description: Legality checked against the official rules as you build, or switched off entirely. Energy curves, matchup plans, and deck codes that other tools can read.
marketing_features_variants_description: Fork a deck to try a change without losing the build that works. Each variant sits on a small graph showing what you added and what you cut.
marketing_features_test_title: Test a deck before you sleeve it
marketing_features_test_description: Deal sample opening hands and try the mulligan. The odds table gives every card's chance of landing in the opening four, and anywhere in your first seven.
marketing_features_box_description: Link a deck to the box you keep it in, then tick each card off as it goes in. Missing and surplus are counted for you, and each row names which copy to pull and which collection it's sitting in.
marketing_features_tournaments_title: From pod night to store event
marketing_features_tournaments_descripti: Swiss pairings for 1v1, pods for three or four players, and fixed teams for 2v2. Deck submission, judges, and deck checks are optional per tournament. Players report their own results from a link, and spectators can follow the standings.
marketing_features_rules_title: The rules, down to the paragraph
marketing_features_rules_description: Every core and tournament rule, filtered as you type. Game terms and cross-references are jump links, so you land on the exact ruling instead of scrolling a PDF. Older versions stay online with the changes since the last one marked up.
marketing_features_tracker_description: Track points and XP in 1v1, 2v2 and FFA games, on one phone.
marketing_features_groups_description: Start a private group for your store crew or your kitchen table. Each group's card sums up what's waiting inside: trades you could make, requests waiting on your answer, and swaps left to confirm. A group can also hold shared collections: a bulk box of spares anyone can take from, or the one collection you and a partner keep together.
marketing_features_trade_match_descripti: Your wishlist meets everyone's tradelists, across the lists people have shared with the group. The group's band leads with the cards you could pick up, so you see the opportunity before you go looking for it.
marketing_features_trade_request_title: Ask for the one you want
marketing_features_trade_request_descrip: Every suggestion says whose copy it is, what condition it is in, and which of your lists asked for it. One press sends the request, and they have a week to answer before it lapses on its own.
marketing_features_trade_reserved_title: They accept, the copy is held
marketing_features_trade_reserved_descri: An accepted trade reserves that exact copy. It stops counting for their decks and drops out of everyone else's suggestions, so two people are never promised the same card.
marketing_features_trade_settle_title: Swap at the table, confirm in the app
marketing_features_trade_settle_descript: You meet up and trade the cards. Then each of you confirms your own half: theirs takes the copy out of their collection, yours puts it into whichever collection you pick. Neither side can log the swap on the other's behalf.
marketing_features_trade_arrived_descrip: The copy is yours, gone from theirs, and off your wishlist. Your decks can use it straight away, and the group's traded count moves. Nothing else in OpenRift spans two people and two collections.
marketing_features_loans_description: Lend cards to a friend and OpenRift remembers who has them. A lent copy stays in your collection but stops counting for decks and trades until you mark it returned.
marketing_features_share_description: Paste a deck link into chat and it unfurls into a preview with the cards, the format, and who built it. The same works for collections, lists, and tier lists. Or download it as an image sized for a post or a vertical story, up to 4K.
marketing_features_discord_title: A bot for your Discord server
marketing_features_discord_description: Type [[card name]] and the bot replies with the art, a link, and prices from TCGplayer, Cardmarket, and CardTrader. Link the server to your group and it also says who has the card on their tradelist. Slash commands unfurl deck codes and look up rulings.
marketing_features_stage_description: Queue up cards and show them two ways: a full-screen view for window capture, or a transparent overlay you paste into OBS as a browser source. Both run off the same queue, and the show is driven from the keyboard, so you can step through a reveal without looking away from the camera.
marketing_features_tier_lists_title: Rank a set on a board
marketing_features_tier_lists_descriptio: Drag cards out of the catalog onto a board and stack them into rows you name yourself, adding and reordering tiers as the argument develops. Share the finished board as a link, download it as an image for a thumbnail, or open it on the Stage and fill it in live while chat weighs in.
marketing_features_chat_description: Paste one line into Nightbot, StreamElements, or Fossabot and viewers can look up any card without leaving chat. The reply carries the stats and a link, and a name that matches nothing comes back as a search instead of an error.
marketing_features_designer_description: Fill in the name, type, domains, stats, and rules text, add your own art, and the card renders as you type. Download it as a PNG or copy it straight to the clipboard.
